text:
My mother had begun keeping her potatoes in the guest bedroom. She said it was the coolest room in the house, which was true, although it was also the room in which I slept. When I arrived that June, six potatoes sat beneath my graduation photograph, each on a square of newspaper.

“They need air,” she said.

“So do I.”

“You can open the window.”

She had made the bed with the yellow sheets, the ones she called good because they had been purchased for a bed my father had built. The bed had outlasted him by eleven years; the sheets seemed determined to do the same to everyone else.

“You look tired,” she said.

“It’s a long drive.”

“You used to do it in three hours.”

“I used to speed.”

“You used to have that little blue car.”

These were, to her, competing explanations.

Downstairs, she had set out ginger biscuits and a dish towel for catching crumbs. The towel had once said SOMEONE IN VERMONT LOVES ME, but only VERMONT remained.

“I brought peaches,” I said.

“Oh, good.”

“They’re ripe.”

“Then we’ll have to eat them.”

She sounded faintly reproachful, as though I had introduced an unnecessary deadline.

At eighty-six, my mother had become smaller and more emphatic. She could no longer reach the serving bowl but had strong views about the new benches downtown, all installed in full sun.

“Who sits there?” she asked. “Lizards?”

She wanted to collect a prescription and return trousers bought at the church sale.

“What’s wrong with them?”

“The pockets are false.”

“Didn’t you notice?”

“They had tissue in them.”

The sophistication of this fraud still impressed her.

I offered to drive, but she said we would walk. At the door, she searched her handbag for her key.

“You’ve got it. I watched you put it in.”

“That doesn’t mean it’s there.”

She found it, touched the brass head, and closed the bag.

Town was twelve minutes away at her old pace and twenty-five at her new one. Outside the house where my friend Alice had grown up, she asked whether I still heard from her.

“Sometimes.”

“Her mother was very kind when your brother broke his arm.”

“That was Mrs. Larkin. Alice’s mother drove us to hospital when I swallowed the coin.”

“Yes,” she said. “She had that awful car.”

I remembered the coin but not the ride. My mother remembered upholstery that burned bare legs. Between us, we could usually assemble an event, though we rarely agreed on its important features.

At the pharmacy, the young man asked for her date of birth.

“You’ve got it written down.”

“He has to ask,” I said.

“I know. I’m telling him where it is.”

While we waited, she chose reading glasses with purple frames. At the register, she asked about a senior discount.

“On Wednesdays,” he said.

“What am I on Saturdays?”

He looked at me. I looked at the blood-pressure machine.

We ate at the café that had once been the hardware store. Drawers for screws and washers now held teas. My father had bought hinges there. My mother disliked the conversion but liked the soup.

She ordered a sandwich without bread.

“Just the filling?” the waitress asked.

“On a plate, please.”

When it arrived, she looked at mine.

“That bread looks nice.”

I gave her half.

At the church hall, the woman accepted the trousers without discussion. My mother seemed disappointed. She had brought the receipt in a plastic envelope and prepared to demonstrate the pockets.

Coming home, we passed my primary school.

“You hated that school,” she said.

“I hated one teacher.”

“Mrs. Vale.”

“Mrs. Vane.”

“She was horrible.”

“You used to say she was very good.”

“Well, I couldn’t have you coming home.”

This was something she had begun doing in old age: offering corrections too late to be of practical use.

At the corner, she took my arm. I shortened my stride without looking at her.

Back home, she wanted the bulb above the stairs changed.

“It went last week. I’ve been leaving the bathroom light on.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I’m telling you now.”

She stood below the stepladder, issuing instructions.

“Not too tight.”

“I know.”

“Your father did them too tight.”

When the bulb came on, she smiled with an unguarded pleasure that made me wish I had more things to mend.

Instead, we sorted a kitchen drawer. This was her proposal, although she objected to nearly everything I tried to remove. There was a key for a vanished suitcase, a thermometer, and several packets of seeds.

“Are you planting these?”

“They’re your father’s.”

On the runner-bean packet, he had written an instruction about soaking them overnight.

“They probably won’t grow.”

“Then they’re not doing any harm in the drawer.”

We kept them.

At four, her neighbor Jean telephoned about the coming heat.

“I’ve lived through summers,” my mother said.

I could hear Jean talking.

“Yes, I’ve got a fan.”

More talking.

“Well, I’m hardly going to run a marathon.”

Afterward, I asked whether she would use the fan.

“If I’m hot.”

“And drink water.”

“I know how to drink water.”

I filled a jug and put it in the refrigerator. The ice trays were empty, so I filled those too.

“Not right to the top,” she said. “They stick.”

For supper, we had eggs and tomatoes on toast. She sliced a peach into a glass dish and poured cream over it. The others went on the windowsill.

“They’ll be too soft tomorrow.”

“Then I’ll have a good breakfast.”

During the news, she fell asleep. I took her cup into the kitchen. When I returned, her eyes were open.

“I was listening.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were going to.”

In the morning, she followed me to the car carrying the remaining peach.

“Take it.”

“You said it was your breakfast.”

“I’ve had toast.”

“I’ve got food at home.”

“Not this peach.”

That evening, she called to ask whether I had arrived.

“Yes.”

“Did you eat the peach?”

“Not yet.”

“You’ll need to.”

I ate it standing over the kitchen sink after we hung up.

For three weeks, our conversations were ordinary. The heat arrived. Jean lent her another fan, which my mother considered excessive. Someone stole a stone birdbath on Orchard Street.

“Was it heavy?” I asked.

“It was stone.”

“Yes, but—”

“Of course it was heavy.”

On a Thursday in July, Jean called from my mother’s kitchen.

“She’s in hospital. She’s all right, but you should come.”

People say this to mean several things at once.

My mother had gone out after lunch to cut the sweet peas. Jean found her sitting on the path, confused and furious, trying to push herself upright with secateurs in one hand. The hospital called it heatstroke. My mother called it a fuss.

She had a line in her arm and a bruise spreading beneath her wrist. Without her glasses, she looked strangely formal, as though waiting to be photographed.

“You needn’t have come tonight,” she said.

“I wanted to.”

“You’ll have hit the traffic.”

A nurse brought water and waited while she drank. My mother obeyed with a politeness she would never have extended to me.

The doctor said she had been severely dehydrated. They were watching her kidneys and would keep her another night, perhaps two.

“She was out there quite a while.”

My mother turned toward the window.

After he left, I asked why she had been gardening in the hottest part of the day.

“They needed cutting.”

“Couldn’t they have waited?”

“They’d gone to seed.”

I began to say something, then stopped. She was rubbing a fold of blanket between finger and thumb.

“Jean says you hadn’t eaten lunch.”

“I had a biscuit.”

“That’s not lunch.”

“It was a large biscuit.”

Her voice was thin, and the joke required more effort than she had expected. I pulled my chair closer.

“What shall I bring tomorrow?”

“My purple glasses. The little comb, not the brush. And the gray trousers in the airing cupboard.”

I knew better than to ask whether they had pockets.

I let myself into the house at eight. The curtains were closed. The air smelled of warm fabric and the water in the vase beside the telephone. Jean had washed the dishes. A cup stood upside down on the draining board.

Outside, the garden was dry except for a dark patch beneath the tap. The sweet peas leaned against their netting. A kitchen chair stood where Jean had left it after getting my mother out of the sun.

I brought it inside.

The house offered no account of what had happened. Her cardigan hung over the banister. On the calendar, she had written CHIROPODIST for the following Tuesday, pressing hard enough to dent the page beneath.

I found the comb and trousers. The purple glasses lay beside her unfinished crossword. One answer had been erased so vigorously that the paper had thinned.

Upstairs, the potatoes had sprouted. Pale stems reached toward the window. I carried them down, then stood uncertainly before putting them in the pantry.

It was still hot after dark. I opened the freezer for ice. The trays were where I had left them a month before, one stacked crookedly on the other. I twisted the top one, and the cubes cracked loose with a sound that startled me.

She had not used any.

I wanted, briefly and unreasonably, to call her. To explain that I had filled them so she could have a cold drink, not so they could sit there while she went into the garden. Then I remembered the hospital cup in her hands, the nurse waiting, my mother taking small obedient sips.

I put three cubes in my glass and returned the tray.

Upstairs, the new bulb illuminated the landing. I left the bathroom light off. In the guest room, I unfolded the yellow sheet, washed and put back after my visit. My bag went beside the dresser.

Before lying down, I removed the potatoes’ newspapers from beneath my graduation photograph. One had stuck to the wood. I dampened it with a towel and rubbed gently until it came away, leaving a clean square in the dust.
